scenarios.title: Create a small restorable content set
scenarios.summary: Validate the whole copy request, preserve exact text and leave a clear recovery index.
scenarios.objective: Accept one to eight filenames as script arguments. Otherwise print Usage: snapshot FILE... on stderr and exit with status 2. The supplied samples use flat relative names of at most 80 UTF-8 bytes, without line breaks; spaces, wildcard characters and leading dashes are literal data. Before inspecting the names, reject an existing snapshot.index with Existing snapshot index on stderr and status 2. Never overwrite a previous recovery set. Validate every name before checking duplicates or files. Empty names, . or .., any name containing /, snapshot.index, and names starting copy- are invalid: print Invalid name on stderr and exit with status 2. Then reject any duplicate requested name with Duplicate request on stderr and status 2. Do this before checking source files or backup destinations. Then inspect requested names in their supplied order. A missing source prints Missing source: NAME on stderr and status 2. An existing copy-NAME prints Backup already exists: copy-NAME on stderr and status 2. Check the source before its destination. Every specified validation failure has no stdout and leaves every file unchanged. Only after all checks succeed, copy each source’s exact text to copy-NAME. Empty contents and all original final newlines are significant. Create snapshot.index with the requested names in their supplied order, one filename plus one newline per record. Print Saved: N files followed by a newline on stdout, with N equal to the number of requested files. Success has status 0 and empty stderr; each error message also ends with a newline. Preserve all source files and all unrelated files, and leave no extra files. This assignment makes content copies in the simulated flat file area; it is not an archive or a metadata-preserving filesystem snapshot.
steps: Copy exact text and verify recovery

initial.source:
# This attempt writes while it is still checking the request and changes final newlines.
for name in "$@"; do
    content=$(cat < "$name")
    printf '%s\n' "$content" > "copy-$name"
    printf '%s\n' "$name" >> snapshot.index
done
printf 'Saved\n'

solution:
if test "$#" -eq 0 || test "$#" -gt 8; then
    printf 'Usage: snapshot FILE...\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
if test -f snapshot.index; then
    printf 'Existing snapshot index\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
names=()
for name in "$@"; do
    case "$name" in
        ''|.|..|*/*|snapshot.index|copy-*) printf 'Invalid name\n' >&2; exit 2 ;;
    esac
    names=("${names[@]}" "$name")
done
seen=()
for name in "${names[@]}"; do
    for earlier in "${seen[@]}"; do
        if test "$name" = "$earlier"; then
            printf 'Duplicate request\n' >&2
            exit 2
        fi
    done
    seen=("${seen[@]}" "$name")
done
for name in "${names[@]}"; do
    if test -f "$name"; then :; else
        printf 'Missing source: %s\n' "$name" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    if test -f "copy-$name"; then
        printf 'Backup already exists: copy-%s\n' "$name" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
done
for name in "${names[@]}"; do
    cat < "$name" > "copy-$name"
done
printf '%s\n' "${names[@]}" > snapshot.index
printf 'Saved: %s files\n' "${#names[@]}"

Supplied filenames are at most 80 UTF-8 bytes with no LF/NUL; this is an explicit input-domain bound, not a claim that the script measures arbitrary filename lengths. Bound backups remain within the 250-byte virtual name limit; binary/NUL data, newline-containing names, directories, metadata/ownership, archives, locks, traps, concurrency and crash/Stop/resource rollback are not modeled. Quoted dense lists in the worked approach are Bash-specific; portable supported alternatives are accepted. Every test starts with its own sample inputs; the simulated files reset for that run. The editor draft persists. No host script, file, command or service is used.
scenarios.explanation: Validate all names and duplicates before any source/destination checks, then finish every file check before opening an output. A dense Bash list retains literal names; a supported nested argument loop is also valid. Direct cat output preserves text without capture stripping final newlines. Write the index only after complete preflight and retain all originals.
hints: Separate request validation from file checks and separate all checks from publication. Which output redirection could create a file too early?
Quote every filename and list expansion. Treat duplicate requests and a destination that already exists as different validation failures.
Copy source text directly instead of passing it through command capture. Build the ordered index only after every source and target is safe.

concepts.title: Keep a small recovery set
concepts.text: A recovery set needs both the copies and a record of which original name each copy belongs to. In this project saved-oak holds oak’s exact text and demo.index records oak on its own line. This is a small content-copy exercise, not tar, a filesystem snapshot or a backup of permissions and ownership.

concepts.title: Inspect the whole request before opening outputs
concepts.text: An output redirection with > can create or truncate its target before the command runs. Validate names, duplicates, every source and every destination first. Do not create an index or a copy while you are still checking a later item. The practice request supplies oak and fern as arguments; the script creates its own names, seen and name variables.

concepts.title: Keep filenames as complete values
concepts.text: Use quoted "$@" to keep each supplied argument intact. The worked Bash list names=("${names[@]}" "$name") rebuilds a dense list with one more complete value; loop over "${names[@]}". The indexed-array assignment and ${names[@]} expansion are Bash-specific; quoted "$@" itself is portable shell. A quoted nested loop can compare earlier names; different supported algorithms are accepted.

concepts.title: Copy text without round-tripping through a variable
concepts.text: cat < "$name" > "saved-$name" sends the file’s text directly to its new destination. Input redirection selects the file directly, even when its name is exactly -. An operand - would instead tell cat to read standard input, even after --. Command capture removes trailing newlines: content=$(cat < "$name") followed by printf can quietly change the copy, even if its displayed words look right.

concepts.title: Make an index you can read back
concepts.text: After validation, printf '%s\n' "${names[@]}" writes one literal name per record. The quoted list preserves spaces and wildcard characters; %s prints each name as data and \n adds its record separator. This simple index deliberately excludes filenames containing a newline. Eight files keeps the project small; execution limits and Stop do not provide automatic rollback.

scenarios.title: Restore an entire validated recovery set
scenarios.summary: Validate every index entry and recovery copy before repairing any target.
scenarios.objective: Accept no script arguments. Otherwise print Usage: restore on stderr and exit with status 2. Then require snapshot.index; if absent, print Missing snapshot index on stderr and exit with status 2. Read snapshot.index as literal filename records in order. Keep surrounding spaces and backslashes; accept a final nonempty filename even when its ending newline is missing. The supplied samples use flat relative names of at most 80 UTF-8 bytes, without line breaks. For each record, first reject an empty name, . or .., any name containing /, snapshot.index, or a name starting copy- with Invalid index entry on stderr and status 2. Then reject a name already encountered with Duplicate index entry: NAME on stderr and status 2. Then require copy-NAME; otherwise print Missing backup: copy-NAME on stderr and exit with status 2. Finally, reject a ninth valid record with Too many snapshot entries on stderr and status 2. Use this record-by-record validation order. After reading the index, reject zero records with Empty snapshot index on stderr and status 2. Complete the entire index and backup validation before changing any file. Every specified validation failure has no stdout and leaves every file unchanged. On success, restore the exact text of each copy-NAME into NAME, replacing an existing target or creating a missing one. Empty backup contents and original final newlines are significant. Print Restored: N files followed by a newline on stdout, with N equal to the number of index records. Success has status 0 and empty stderr; each error message also ends with a newline. Keep snapshot.index and every recovery copy byte-for-byte unchanged. Preserve all unselected files and leave no extra files. This is bounded content recovery; no archive extraction, metadata, locking or crash-safety claim is made.
steps: Copy exact text and verify recovery

# This attempt loses padded/EOF records and writes before validating the whole index.

    cat < "copy-$name" > "$name"
done < snapshot.index

cases.name: Unexpected arguments fail before inspecting files

solution:
if test "$#" -ne 0; then
    printf 'Usage: restore\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
if test -f snapshot.index; then :; else
    printf 'Missing snapshot index\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
names=()
while IFS= read -r name || test -n "$name"; do
    case "$name" in
        ''|.|..|*/*|snapshot.index|copy-*) printf 'Invalid index entry\n' >&2; exit 2 ;;
    esac
    for earlier in "${names[@]}"; do
        if test "$name" = "$earlier"; then
            printf 'Duplicate index entry: %s\n' "$name" >&2
            exit 2
        fi
    done
    if test -f "copy-$name"; then :; else
        printf 'Missing backup: copy-%s\n' "$name" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    names=("${names[@]}" "$name")
    if test "${#names[@]}" -gt 8; then
        printf 'Too many snapshot entries\n' >&2
        exit 2
    fi
done < snapshot.index
if test "${#names[@]}" -eq 0; then
    printf 'Empty snapshot index\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
for name in "${names[@]}"; do
    cat < "copy-$name" > "$name"
done
printf 'Restored: %s files\n' "${#names[@]}"

Do not move or remove the recovery copies. Read each copy into its target only after all required copies and records passed validation.

concepts.title: A copy is useful only if it can be restored
concepts.text: Read the existing index to find what to restore, then use the corresponding saved-NAME file. The separate practice index names oak and fern; the lab supplies those files and the script creates its own names and name variables. Restoring must not consume or rewrite the recovery copies or the index.

concepts.title: Read literal records, including the last one
concepts.text: while IFS= read -r name || test -n "$name" keeps surrounding spaces and backslashes and handles a final nonempty record without a newline. End the loop with done < demo.index so its collected list remains in the caller. A pipeline loop isolates variable changes in this simulator’s disclosed shell subset.

concepts.title: Validate the complete plan before the first repair
concepts.text: For each record, check its name, duplicates, the required recovery copy and the eight-file bound in the stated order. After the loop, reject an empty index. Collect names before publishing anything: a missing copy in the last record must leave every earlier target untouched too.

concepts.title: Restore exact text and preserve the evidence
concepts.text: cat < "saved-$name" > "$name" restores bytes without command capture stripping final newlines. Keep both operands quoted, including when names contain spaces, wildcards or a leading dash. Compare the final file text as well as stdout/status; a reassuring success message alone does not prove recovery.

concepts.title: A bounded plan is not a transaction
concepts.text: The worked names list and its quoted expansion are Bash-specific; a supported two-pass loop is an alternative. This virtual project has no directories, archive extraction, metadata, real locks or crash recovery. Complete preflight protects the specified validation-error cases; Stop, resource exhaustion and unexpected failures do not automatically undo earlier writes.
